Gloucester is the Earl of Gloucester in King Lear and the protagonist of the play's parallel plot, a tragedy within a tragedy. Deceived by his bastard son Edmund into believing his legitimate heir Edgar has betrayed him, Gloucester suffers a catastrophe that mirrors and intensifies Lear's own downfall, ultimately suggesting that blindness—literal and metaphorical—is the human condition in Shakespeare's darkest play.

A subsidiary noble whose subplot mirrors Lear's central tragedy, both Gloucester and Lear are deceived by children they trust, abandoned by those they favor, and destroyed by misjudgment of character. Gloucester is easily manipulated by Edmund, who exploits his father's credulity and paternal anxiety to convince him that Edgar, his legitimate son, plots against him. He is initially sympathetic to Edmund partly because Edmund is illegitimate but charming, while Edgar is legitimate but bookish and reserved. This shows how superficial traits can blind a parent to deeper truths.

After attempting to protect Lear when the king is cast out, Gloucester is tortured by Regan and Goneril. In a scene of almost unwatchable brutality, his eyes are plucked out on stage. His literal blindness becomes the play's central metaphor: he was metaphorically blind to Edmund's villainy and Edgar's loyalty while sighted, and achieves spiritual sight only after losing his eyes. After being blinded and cast out, he wanders in despair and eventually attempts suicide by leaping from Dover Cliff, though he is actually saved by the disguised Edgar.

The revelation that Edgar has been wandering mad beside him while he thought him a traitor creates a final tragic recognition. His suffering at the hands of his children parallels Lear's but reaches a greater extreme. While Lear retains his inner sight and rage, Gloucester is literally maimed and spiritually broken before redemption. In the final act, he learns that Edgar is alive and legitimate just before dying, suggesting that understanding often arrives too late to prevent catastrophe. The subplot deepens Lear's tragedy: Gloucester's blindness makes the play's central metaphor—seeing and not seeing moral truth—literal and visceral.
